body.text: C01–C03 are the three core information-security objectives, collectively called the CIA triad. C04 concerns evidence and attribution, while C05 concerns data exposure closely related to confidentiality.

body.name: ciaobjectives
body.caption: CIA objectives and two related concepts
body.description: The three upper items are parallel security objectives. Non-repudiation concerns evidence; cleartext concerns data representation and exposure. They are not a fourth and fifth CIA objective.

items.title: C03 · Availability
items.body: Can authorized users use it when needed?

items.title: C05 · Cleartext
items.body: Is readable data exposed across an inappropriate trust boundary?

body.text: Suppose an engineer uses a process-management system in a semiconductor fab:

items: People unrelated to a project must not read the customer’s chip designs: confidentiality.
Unauthorized personnel must not secretly change process parameters: integrity.
Production must receive the required data when needed: availability.
Important parameter changes must be traceable to their operators and approval records: non-repudiation.
Confidential data sent over a network needs suitable protection against third parties reading it as cleartext.

body.text: These concepts interact. For example, a correctly authenticated encrypted connection can help protect both the confidentiality and integrity of data in transit.
M01-01 · The CIA triad
1. What is confidentiality?
Confidentiality means that only authorized people or systems may access or learn particular information.
Imagine that you manage research and development at a semiconductor company and hold technical information about its next-generation process.
Different people may receive different permissions:

items: Process engineers may read the process data they are responsible for.
The R&D manager may view more comprehensive technical information.
Contracted equipment-maintenance personnel receive only the minimum information necessary for maintenance.
Unauthorized personnel must not read this information.

body.text: Confidentiality is about deciding who may see which information according to authorization. It does not require making every piece of information inaccessible to everyone.
NIST defines confidentiality around preserving authorized restrictions on access and disclosure, including personal privacy and proprietary information.
2. Taiwan’s semiconductor industry: why protect chip designs and process data?
Suppose a semiconductor company holds an unpublished advanced-process recipe that would be highly valuable to competitors.
An employee forwarding that recipe to a personal mailbox may raise trade-secret protection issues as well as internal-management concerns.
Legal basis: Article 2 of Taiwan’s Trade Secrets Act.
A trade secret must meet three statutory requirements:
1. Secrecy: the information is not generally known to people involved with that type of information.
2. Economic value: its secrecy gives it actual or potential economic value.
3. Reasonable secrecy measures: the owner has actually adopted reasonable protective measures.

Authentication, access permissions, document classification, confidentiality agreements and encryption can contribute to reasonable secrecy measures. Taiwan’s Intellectual Property Office also identifies such practices.
Published corporate practice: TSMC’s information-security policies.

TSMC’s [2023 annual report](https://investor.tsmc.com/static/annualReports/2023/english/pdf/2023_tsmc_ar_e_ch5.pdf) discusses ISO 27001 and customer-information protection. Its [2024 customer-information article](https://esg.tsmc.com/en-US/articles/298) describes assessment and audit, system design, security controls and mechanism review. These disclosures belong to particular reporting years. This lesson has not obtained and verified every certificate valid in 2026; ISO/IEC 15408 site certification must not be conflated with ISO 27001.
In semiconductor manufacturing, confidentiality supports the company’s competitive position and requires participation beyond the IT department.
3. Silicon Valley technology companies: why can’t engineers freely read production data?
Suppose an AI company stores business documents uploaded by customers. An engineer’s system-maintenance responsibilities do not automatically authorize reading every customer document.
A suitable system restricts data access, protects storage and transmission, and records sensitive operations.
Technical framework: NIST CSF 2.0.

items: PR.DS-01: protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of data at rest.
PR.DS-02: protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of data in transit.

body.text: Organizations can adopt this cybersecurity framework. It is not a certification that every Silicon Valley company is legally required to obtain.
California law: Civil Code §1798.81.5(b).

For businesses within its scope, this provision requires reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the nature of personal information, protecting it against unauthorized access, use, modification or disclosure. A legal requirement and NIST technical guidance have different authority.
4. Taiwan’s financial industry: why restrict customer-record access?
Suppose a bank employee, out of personal curiosity, looks up a customer’s deposit balance and discloses it to a friend.
This concerns confidentiality even if the data is accurate and the bank’s systems operate normally.
Regulatory basis: the FSC’s Implementation Rules of Internal Audit and Internal Control System of Financial Holding Companies and Banking Industries.

Article 12 includes customer-data confidentiality in internal-control policies and procedures. Article 25 assigns the dedicated information-security unit responsibility for overseeing implementation and ensuring confidentiality, integrity and availability.
5. Reasoning cues for CEH questions
Consider confidentiality first when the scenario describes:

items: Unauthorized disclosure: information revealed without permission.
Information leakage: protected information escapes its intended boundary.
Eavesdropping: another party listens to communication.
Data exfiltration: information is extracted or stolen.
Unauthorized reading: someone reads information without permission.

body.text: Ask: did someone who should not have access obtain the information?
If so, confidentiality is usually the primary security property involved.
M01-01 · The CIA triad
1. What is integrity?
Integrity means that information remains in its intended correct state, protected from unauthorized or improper modification and destruction.
Integrity asks a different question from confidentiality.
Suppose a bank-transfer instruction originally contains the following amount:

body.name: transactiontampering
body.caption: Transaction integrity: unauthorized amount change
body.description: The two states compare the original instruction with tampered content, not two executed transfers. The amount changes from NT$10,000 to NT$100,000.

body.text: Even if an attacker never reads other customers’ records, successfully changing this transfer instruction directly compromises integrity.
NIST describes data integrity as the property that data has not been changed without authorization after its creation, transmission or storage.
Integrity does not prohibit every change.

A properly authenticated customer changing their own mailing address is an authorized operation consistent with integrity. An attacker impersonating that customer and changing the address without permission creates an integrity problem.
2. Taiwan’s semiconductor industry: what happens when process parameters are altered?
Suppose engineers approved equipment parameters at a fab, but an attacker gains control of the equipment and secretly changes them.
The equipment might keep running and confidential documents might remain undisclosed, while production results deviate from expectations.
The primary issue concerns the integrity of process data and control commands. If the incident also stops production, availability is affected too.
Industry reference: SEMI E187 — Specification for Cybersecurity of Fab Equipment.
SEMI E187 addresses cybersecurity of semiconductor fab equipment, including operating-system support, network security, endpoint protection and security monitoring.

SEMI describes standards work involving its Taiwan, North America and Japan technical committees. Equipment-security controls can help reduce process risks caused by unauthorized operations and malware.
SEMI E187 concerns equipment cybersecurity. The company’s own process and equipment controls must implement specific parameter approvals, change authorization and integrity verification.
3. Silicon Valley: why verify software-update integrity?
Suppose a US software company releases a legitimate installer, but an attacker replaces the file on its download site with a malicious version.
Users may download it believing it is the official software.
Engineering controls include:

items: Cryptographic hash: produce a digest to help detect file changes.
Digital signature: verify the signing source and integrity since signing.
Access control: restrict who may modify release artifacts.
Change management: track changes through review and version control.

body.text: NIST CSF 2.0 implementation examples for PR.DS-01 include verifying software signatures to establish integrity.
The trustworthiness of the verification information matters:

A plain hash helps compare files. If an attacker can replace both the file and its published hash, however, the user can still be deceived. Verification digests or signatures therefore need a trusted source.
4. Taiwan’s financial industry: protecting transaction-instruction integrity
For the transfer example, an institution must establish both who logged in and whether the instruction received by its backend matches what the customer actually entered.

Articles 5 and 6 of the current [Electronic Payment Institutions Information System Standards and Security Control Guidelines](https://epa.org.tw/uploads/regulations/pdfs/01M47H2X8FK89E4RTGBCPV9WSW.pdf) address message protection. Article 11, paragraph 1, item 4 addresses consistency between payment instructions entered by users and received by the system. The similarly named regulations cited in the supplied text were repealed on April 25, 2023; this lesson uses the September 29, 2026 association guidelines.

These association guidelines are established under Article 32, paragraph 2 of the Act Governing Electronic Payment Institutions. Their scope differs from banking rules for electronic banking. Identify the institution, transaction type, security design and version before mapping integrity controls to specific requirements.
5. Reasoning cues for CEH questions
Check whether the question describes:

items: Unauthorized modification.
Tampering.
Data corruption.
Unauthorized deletion.
An altered transaction.

body.text: These cues point first to integrity.
Ask: was information changed without authorization, or did it lose its intended trustworthy state?
M01-01 · The CIA triad
1. What is availability?
Availability means that authorized users can reliably obtain information or use services when needed.
Suppose your bank account contains money and its records are accurate, but you cannot log in to online banking when you urgently need to make a transfer.
What failed in this situation?
The information need not have been stolen or changed. The immediate problem is that you cannot use the service when needed.
This is an availability problem.
NIST defines availability around timely and reliable access to and use of information.
2. Taiwan’s semiconductor industry: why does fab availability matter?
Suppose a fab’s manufacturing execution system, or MES, suddenly stops working.
Engineers may lose access to production-lot information, equipment status and process-operation data, affecting factory operations.
The primary issue is the availability of systems required for production.
In semiconductor manufacturing, availability also requires equipment, networks and manufacturing processes to keep working together, beyond individual computers remaining operational.
Industry context:

SEMI E187 addresses operating systems, networks, endpoint protection and security monitoring. TSMC has also publicly described malware protection, network segmentation and limiting virus propagation between equipment and fabs. Such controls can reduce the risk of security incidents interrupting production systems.
3. Silicon Valley: how do cloud services maintain availability?
Suppose a Silicon Valley SaaS company provides an enterprise AI service.

body.name: serviceavailability
body.caption: Single points of failure and redundant nodes
body.description: Upper group: a user reaches one failed server. Lower group: another user reaches parallel servers A and B through traffic distribution; A does not forward to B. Distributor, data-layer and common-mode failures require separate design.

items.title: Single server fails
items.body: A single point of failure may interrupt service

body.text: Technical framework: NIST CSF 2.0.
PR.IR-03 addresses resilience in normal and adverse conditions. Implementation examples include avoiding single points of failure, load balancing, redundant storage and backup power.
PR.IR-04 focuses on maintaining sufficient compute, storage, power and network capacity.
These measures connect high availability with resilience.
High availability focuses on reducing service interruptions. Resilience additionally concerns maintaining necessary functions and recovering during failures or attacks.
4. Taiwan’s financial industry: service interruption extends beyond IT
Suppose malicious traffic overwhelms online banking, preventing users from logging in or transferring funds.
The primary impact of this denial-of-service, or DoS, scenario is usually availability.
Article 12 of the FSC banking internal-control rules includes business-continuity management. Article 25 covers the availability of systems and services and security-incident response.
Two practical objectives help plan recovery:

rows: How soon after an interruption should service be restored?
How much recent data loss is tolerable? For an assumed RPO of 15 minutes, the recovery point should be no more than 15 minutes before the interruption.

body.text: A bank needs to establish both how to restart systems and whether transaction records have been restored correctly. Availability and integrity often require coordinated controls.
5. Reasoning cues for CEH questions
Service disruption, DoS, DDoS, system outage, resource exhaustion and an inaccessible system point first to availability.
Ask: are authorized users unable to obtain the service when they need it?
M01-07 · Security governance and evidence conditions
1. What is non-repudiation?
Non-repudiation uses reliable evidence to make important actions, their origin and attribution verifiable.
Suppose a semiconductor company employs two engineers.
An important process document is approved and enters production. A problem is later discovered, and the responsible person says:
“I did not approve this.”
How should the company verify what happened?
The person’s name appearing in a database may be insufficient evidence.
A stronger evidence package includes operator identity, the approved content, operation time, a trustworthy signature and protected audit records.
NIST describes non-repudiation as establishing evidence that resists false denial of actions such as creating a document, sending a message or approving information.
2. How does non-repudiation differ from integrity?
Consider an electronic contract:

items: Integrity: verify that the contract content has not been improperly changed.
Non-repudiation: provide verifiable evidence supporting attribution to a particular signer.

body.text: These are related but distinct questions.
Information-security frameworks also treat non-repudiation as an assurance related to integrity and authenticity.
3. How can digital signatures establish evidence?

body.name: signatureevidence
body.caption: Digital signatures: creating and verifying evidence
body.description: A typical conceptual flow; actual computation differs by algorithm. Attribution also requires trusted certificates, private-key protection, time and audit evidence. A name in a database is insufficient.

items.title: Original electronic document
items.body: For example, an approved process-change record

items.title: Generate a cryptographic hash
items.body: Map the document to a fixed-length digest

items.title: Sign using the private key
items.body: Create a signature with a key controlled by the signer

items.title: Verify signature and identity
items.body: Use the public key with certificates, time and audit records

body.text: A digital signature can provide evidence verifiable by a third party. Attribution also requires trustworthy certificates, private-key protection and a complete signing process.
4. References for the three industries
Taiwan’s semiconductor industry: signing and tracing process changes.
A company can maintain digital approvals for critical process changes, combining signatures, identity verification and audit records protected against arbitrary modification.

Article 2 of Taiwan’s [Electronic Signatures Act](https://law.moj.gov.tw/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?pcode=J0080037) defines electronic and digital signatures. Article 4 addresses functional equivalence and legal effect when the statutory requirements are met. Article 6 presumes a personal signature or seal only when the certificate comes from an authorized certification authority and remains within its validity period and permitted scope. Successful technical verification still requires checking these legal conditions.
Silicon Valley: proving the source of important software releases.
Software companies can sign releases so users can verify artifacts and signing sources. NIST FIPS 186-5 describes third-party-verifiable origin and integrity as properties supporting non-repudiation.
Taiwan’s financial industry: preserving electronic-transaction evidence.

Articles 5 and 6 of the current electronic-payment association guidelines address non-repudiation according to the applicable security design. Article 10 addresses certificate signing and verification and private-key protection for linked-deposit-account payments. Check signatures, certificates and records against the transaction type; Articles 7–9 of the repealed regulations are not current clause references.

The Bankers Association also lists its Security Control Guidelines for Financial Institutions Using Electronic Signature Mechanisms, announced on its website on May 18, 2026, as a specialized reference for relevant banking operations.
5. Reasoning cues for CEH questions
Denial of signing or sending a message, disputed transaction attribution, digital-signature evidence and verifiable signing records usually concern non-repudiation.
Encryption, hashes and digital signatures provide different capabilities.

heading: 6 | C05: Cleartext transmission and information exposure

body.text: M01-01 · Confidentiality and data-in-transit risk
1. What is cleartext?
Cleartext is information in a directly readable, understandable form without encryption protecting its contents.
For example, a third party able to intercept unencrypted bank-account information on an untrusted network may read its contents directly.
NIST’s glossary describes cleartext as unencrypted information and identifies plaintext as a related term.
2. Why is HTTPS generally more suitable than HTTP for sensitive data?

body.name: transportprotection
body.caption: HTTP and HTTPS: protecting data in transit
body.description: Upper row: HTTP without additional encryption may reveal content to an interceptor. Lower row: a correctly established HTTPS/TLS channel protects confidentiality and integrity. These are independent comparisons with no connection between the rows.

items.title: HTTP server
items.body: An interceptor may read captured content

body.text: RFC 8446 was the original TLS 1.3 specification. [RFC 9846](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9846), published in July 2026, supersedes it. TLS provides authentication, confidentiality and integrity. HTTPS requires correct server validation and TLS establishment; endpoints, applications and key management still need protection.
HTTPS uses TLS to establish a protected communication channel.
Two distinctions are easy to overlook.
First, Base64 is not encryption.
A password encoded with Base64 can be decoded by anyone who knows the encoding. Encoding supports data representation and transport compatibility; it does not provide confidentiality.
Second, the presence of cleartext does not by itself prove a confidentiality incident.

An authorized user reading a decrypted document in a secure environment is part of normal use. The security issue depends on whether readable data crosses an inappropriate trust boundary or reaches an unauthorized party.
3. Applications in the three industries

rows: Protect customer chip-design data crossing systems with encryption and access controls appropriate to its sensitivity
Trade Secrets Act, Article 2; TSMC’s published data-protection and ISMS practices
Use HTTPS/TLS for customer data, validating server identity and channel protection
RFC 8446, superseded by RFC 9846; NIST CSF 2.0 PR.DS-02
Electronic-payment institutions protect sensitive Internet transmissions with encryption throughout
Current electronic-payment association guidelines, Article 11, paragraph 1, item 1

body.text: For banks, the Bankers Association’s specialized electronic-banking security-control guidelines were announced on its website on February 5, 2026. They are industry self-regulatory standards.
4. Reasoning cues for CEH questions
For sensitive data, cleartext transmission, unencrypted traffic, packet sniffing and eavesdropping, first ask whether an attacker can read transmitted content without authorization.
Cleartext transmission describes a risk scenario. Its most direct CIA objective is usually confidentiality.

rows: A signer denies an approved transaction
Sensitive data crosses an unsafe network in readable form

body.text: Compare the purposes of common technical controls:

rows: Produce a digest for integrity comparison
Use a shared secret to verify integrity and message origin
Verify signing origin and integrity, supporting non-repudiation
Support data recovery and service availability

body.text: One control can support several objectives. TLS 1.3 concerns channel confidentiality, integrity and authentication; digital signatures concern both integrity and origin evidence.
The following references are grouped by their authority and can support later CEH M01–M20 study.

rows: Historical TSMC annual-report disclosures of ISO 27001 and information-security policies; verify actual certificate scope and validity
IETF RFC 8446, superseded by RFC 9846 — TLS 1.3
FSC banking internal-control rules, Articles 12 and 25
Current electronic-payment information-system and security-control guidelines, Articles 5, 6, 10 and 11

body.text: Article 55 of the May 6, 2026 revision of the [banking internal-control rules](https://law.fsc.gov.tw/LawContent.aspx?id=FL049894) leaves the commencement of Articles 44–47 to a separate determination; the other provisions take effect upon promulgation. Articles 12 and 25 used here are outside that deferred group. Formal reviews must still identify the institution, business and applicable version.

heading: 9 | Understanding check: integrate the five concepts

body.text: This is a new teaching scenario, not an original question from the attachment. Try answering before consulting references; model answers are withheld.

A Taiwanese semiconductor company partners with a Silicon Valley AI company to build an automated process-analysis system. They exchange design information through a cloud platform, with project financing provided by a Taiwanese bank.
Five events occur:
1. An engineer at the AI company, without project authorization, reads the semiconductor company’s confidential design documents.
2. An attacker changes process parameters sent by the AI system to the fab.
3. DDoS interrupts the cloud service, preventing the fab from obtaining real-time analysis results.
4. A manager denies approving a critical process change, but the system retains a valid digital signature.
5. The companies transmit confidential customer technical documents through unencrypted HTTP.
Answer three questions:
Q1. Which C01–C05 concept most directly matches each event? Which CIA objective does event 5 primarily threaten?
Q2. Which controls would you choose to protect integrity against event 2? Why is data encryption alone insufficient?

Q3. If the system is reviewed by Taiwanese semiconductor customers, US enterprise customers and Taiwanese financial institutions, which three categories of laws or standards would you cite for design and audit requirements?
